text: The bus left Asha at the bottom of the harbour road just as the light came on in the tower. For a second she forgot why she had come home. Then she remembered that the light should not be on at all, because the man who lit it every evening for forty years had been buried that morning.

Mrs D'Souza from the bakery pressed a paper bag of rusks into Asha's hands and would not meet her eyes. 'Your grandfather was a good man,' she said, too quickly. 'Whatever people say.' Asha had not heard anyone say anything yet.

The logbook was where he had always kept it, on the shelf beside the kettle. Every night was there in his small, slanted writing: the weather, the ships, the hour the lamp was lit. Every night except for eleven pages in the spring of 1998, which had been cut out so neatly that she almost missed it.

Inspector Fernandes listened to all of it and then closed his notebook. 'Old men fall down stairs, Miss Asha. It is sad, but it is not a mystery.' On her way out she noticed he had not written anything down.

From the top of the lighthouse the whole town looked small and harmless, the fishing boats lined up like toys. Asha counted the houses whose windows faced the tower. Six. Six families who could see the light every night, and who would have noticed if it went out.

The key did not fit the lighthouse door, or the shed, or the old sea chest. It was only when she held it up against the lamp that she saw the number scratched into it, and understood where her grandfather had hidden the missing pages.
Wren had cleaned every stall in the royal stables twice before anyone noticed the crown was missing. By then the crow on the rafter had already decided she was the one who would carry it.

Sir Aldous had not worn his armour in six years, and it showed. The straps had stiffened and the breastplate no longer met in the middle. 'A quest,' he said, as if tasting a word he had once liked. 'With a stable girl and a bird.'

The crown was warm, which crowns should not be. Every night Wren wrapped it in her spare shirt and every morning it had worked its way to the top of the pack, as if it wanted to see where they were going.

The ferryman would take silver or a story, he said, and since they had no silver Aldous told him about the battle at the Grey Ford. Wren noticed he told it differently from the songs. In his version, he was the one who ran.
Snow came early to the mountain pass. Corvin the crow refused to fly in it and rode on Wren's shoulder, muttering. 'Eleven days to the solstice,' he said. 'Ten if we stop complaining.'
At the gates of the old city the crown finally spoke, in a voice that sounded a little like Wren's own. It did not ask to be returned. It asked to be worn.
The orchard had not been pruned in two years and the branches leaned over the path as if they were listening. Maya parked behind Ruth's car and sat for a long time before she went in.

There were three cups in the drying rack, the blue ones with the chipped handles. Their mother had always set out three, even after they had all moved away, even on the years nobody came home for the harvest.
Ruth had the buyer's letter folded in her pocket and kept touching it, the way you touch a sore tooth. Anna, the youngest, said what everyone was thinking: 'You've already decided, haven't you?'

They picked in silence that first week, each sister taking a different row. By the end of it their hands knew the work again before they did, and the silence started to feel less like an argument and more like company.
The last crate was the heaviest. They carried it together, one on each side and Anna at the back, and nobody mentioned the letter.
